THE WATCH

The prisoner of war walked three miles with a limp before he found the address. He put the gold watch in the boy's small hands and said his father had kept it wound through every year of captivity, that it had been the only clean thing in that place. The boy, who would grow up to be called Denny, held it like something that might stop existing if he looked away.

Years later Denny hid in a motel room with Marielle, boxing money folded in his sock, and asked her where his father's watch was. She went pale. Left it on the dresser, she said. He was already pulling his boots on.

He drove back to the flat alone. The submachine gun on the kitchen counter belonged to nobody he expected — Rollo, waiting there for reasons that no longer mattered, took three rounds before he understood what was happening. Denny found the watch under a newspaper, put it in his pocket, and walked out past the body without looking at it twice.

*

Rollo and Marcus spent most drives arguing. That week it was foreign drug laws, and what a hamburger was called in France, and neither of them changed the other's mind. Outside Tobin's door they argued about whether a foot massage was worth killing a man for; Marcus said nothing was worth killing a man for, then recited scripture anyway and shot Tobin twice for double-crossing Otis. They took the briefcase. A fourth man burst from the bathroom and emptied a revolver at them and hit nothing, which Marcus called proof of God's mercy on somebody.

In the car Rollo's gun went off by accident and took the top of Del's head clean away. They sat in stunned silence until Marcus said they'd better call Warren.

Warren's fixer met them in the driveway, directed the hosing-down of the seats, and handed them each a clean shirt like a maître d'.

They delivered the briefcase to Otis at the bar, where Otis was in the back paying Denny to go down in the fifth round, counting bills into his palm like a man counting out a life.

Rollo bought his heroin from Kip that same night and shot up before taking Nadia, Otis's wife, to the diner with the fifties theme, where they won the dance contest under a spinning disco ball shaped like a hamburger. Later, at Kip's, Nadia snorted the last of it and stopped breathing until the needle of adrenaline went into her chest and brought her back with a scream.

*

On a Tuesday two small-time robbers sat over eggs and coffee and decided, with no forethought at all, to rob the diner they were sitting in. Marcus, waiting there with the briefcase for a meeting that hadn't happened yet, talked the gunman down, handed over his own wallet, and let the couple walk out into the rain still holding the register drawer.

Denny, in the ring, took Otis's money and then didn't go down — he beat his opponent bloody and killed him with a final shot that no one in the crowd would forget, then fled in a taxi before the referee had finished counting.

Otis and Denny found each other in the street weeks later, crashed the car between them, and woke up prisoners in the basement of a pawnshop, wrists tied to a radiator. While one of the captors was busy raping Otis in the corner, Denny worked his hands loose, took a sword down off the wall where it had hung as decoration, and ended it. Otis, bleeding, said they were square, so long as Denny left town and never sent word.

Denny went back for Marielle. He took a motorcycle from the pawnshop floor, its keys still in the ignition, and they rode out past the city limits at dawn, his father's watch ticking faithfully in his jacket pocket, the only clean thing either of them owned.

Tobias woke on an ordinary morning with no memory that Ivy ever existed, and the first strange thing he did was skip work on an impulse he couldn't account for. He took the train to the end of the line, to the seaside town, and there, on the frozen sand, he met a woman named Ivy who was laughing at the ice like she'd invented it.

Inside his own head, hours earlier, he had watched the ugliest memories dissolve one by one — the fight over the dented car, the accusations, the last look she gave him before walking out for good. He had let those go gladly. But reaching the ones he loved — the frozen river, the noodle house, the drive-in — he'd changed his mind and tried to smuggle her into memories she was never part of, hiding her inside scenes that had nothing to do with her, hoping some trace would survive the wreckage.

Ivy and Tobias drove back to the city together, and she invited him up to her flat, and he went, not knowing why it felt like coming home.

Before that night, Dell and the receptionist Rosa had gotten high on Tobias's bed and lost track of the procedure entirely, his memory-map sprawling off its careful lines, and Dr. Hallam had to be called in at two in the morning to re-route the erasure by hand. Rosa, giddy and reckless, kissed him in the hallway — until his wife arrived and told her, flatly, that this wasn't the first time, that Rosa's own affair with Hallam had already been erased from her once before.

Ivy listened to a tape of her own voice, recorded from some earlier session Tobias didn't yet understand, tearing into a man she no longer recognized as him. She ran from the flat. She came back an hour later, sat on the stairs, and told him they should try anyway.

Before the erasure had even begun, Tobias had spent an evening boxing up every object that connected to Ivy — ticket stubs, a scarf, a chipped noodle bowl — so the clinic could map the memories fused to them. Dell and a young technician named Peck ran the overnight procedure in his flat while he lay there sedated, and Peck, quietly, without anyone noticing, slid a few of the mementos into his own pocket.

That had followed the day Nina and Grady showed Tobias a form letter — Ivy's memory of him, professionally deleted — and he had gone straight to Dr. Hallam's office and demanded the same be done to him.

Which had followed the day he'd walked into the bookshop where Ivy worked and found her treating him like a stranger, flirting easily with a young man who turned out to be Peck, the same one who would later steal his mementos to use on her.

Before that: the dent in the car, the drunken night, Ivy's voice breaking against his silence, the fight that ended with her walking out the door for the last time. Before that, months of curdling — her drinking, his withholding, the slow poison of two people who loved each other badly. Before that, two years of falling — the ice on the river, the noodle house steaming their glasses, the drive-in screen flickering blue on their faces. Before that, the beginning: a beach party at the end of the rail line, and an empty house on the shore they broke into on a dare, laughing, unable to stop touching each other's sleeves.

And in the last surviving memory inside his erasure, the one Hallam's rerouting couldn't quite kill, they stood in that same empty house years later, saying goodbye, and Ivy told him to meet her at the beach — words that meant nothing to the machines mapping his brain, and everything to whatever part of him refused to let go.

Rosa quit the clinic not long after, unable to look at Hallam again, and mailed every patient's files and session tapes back to them unopened, a small act of penance.

Which is how Tobias and Ivy came to sit on her floor months later, replaying their own recorded voices tearing each other apart, and choosing, anyway, to stay.

The heart arrives before the man who owns it does, which is the sort of thing you learn to accept when your life has become a series of borrowed things. Aaron Vale wakes into a body that no longer wants to stop, and the first thought that comes to him, ridiculous and immediate, is that somewhere a family has just finished grieving so that he could finish nothing at all.

Della is not there when he wakes. She had been there for the part before, the part where the doctors told him weeks, not months, and she had leaned over the hospital bed with the frozen vials already scheduled, already paid for, and asked him to give her something of himself that would outlast the failing muscle in his chest. He remembers that more clearly than he remembers the surgery. He remembers telling her he would think about it, and thinking, even then, that thinking about it was a kind of lie they both allowed him.

He does not tell her, later, when he is well enough to leave her, that the reason has anything to do with the heart. He simply says he does not want the child. She asks how he can say that after everything, and he doesn't have an answer that isn't the truth, which is that he has started listening to the thing beating in him as if it might speak.

He hires a man to find out whose it was. This takes very little time and no wisdom at all — a woman's name, an address, a photograph of a woman standing at the edge of a public pool with her arms crossed over herself like a person guarding a wound. Lena Ward. He goes there before he has decided to go there, watches her for three visits before he lets himself be seen, and when he finally speaks to her at the pool's edge it is with the specific, terrible ease of a man who has already given up pretending this is coincidence.

She does not know, at first, why she lets him stay. Perhaps because she has already spent a long stretch of nights putting cocaine into the hollow her husband and daughters left, methodically, like a woman filling in a grave with her own hands, and Aaron does not ask her to explain any of it. When he tells her — finally, stupidly, in her kitchen with the tap running — that the heart under his ribs used to belong to her husband, she throws a glass at him and orders him out. Two days later she lets him back in, and neither of them discusses why.

What she wants, once she has him back, is Wes Tarrow dead. She says it like a shopping list item. Wes had walked into a station and confessed, had gone back to prison for it, had lost his faith and his wife and his temper along with his freedom, and none of that undoing matters to her at all. Aaron buys a gun because it is easier than telling her no.

He finds Wes at a motel off a highway that seems designed for men trying to disappear, and he does shoot him, but his hand fails him the way his heart once failed him, and the wound is only a wound. He tells Wes to run.

Wes doesn't run. He follows them instead, finds their room, and asks, with the flat calm of a man long past bargaining, for Aaron to finish what he started. Aaron turns the gun on himself.

There is a hospital again, fluorescent and indifferent, and this time it is Lena and Wes standing over him rather than Della, and the heart that once belonged to Doug Ward stutters out for good in a chest that was never really built to keep it.

Wes goes home, to Nita, to whatever is left of the family he abandoned. Lena drives home alone, carrying a child that will have no father anyone can name without difficulty, carrying also whatever is left of a heart she was never given the chance to bury properly the first time.

The gun was still warm when Martin photographed the second body, though he could not have said how it got that way. He crouched over the man on the concrete floor, a bullet hole above the left eye, and slid the photograph into his shirt pocket next to a dozen others just like it, men he did not remember meeting.

Twenty minutes earlier, at the registry desk lit green by a computer screen, a woman with a split lip and a name he'd written on his arm—Corinne—had handed him a printout. *Roy Mercer,* it said, beside a plate number tattooed six inches from his knee. "That's him," she said. "That's the one who's been lying to you."

Before that, Martin had a man named Vance zip-tied in the trunk light of a motel bathroom, knuckles split, driving him to the county line at gunpoint because Corinne had come home bruised and sobbing his name. He didn't ask why she wanted this. His notes told him to trust her.

Before that: Corinne hiding every pen in her house, laughing when he couldn't find one to write with, needling him with a fingernail until he struck her once, hard, and she smiled through the pain like she'd won something.

Before that: Corinne recognizing a dead man's suit on a stranger's back, a dead man's car in her lot, and pouring him a beer her bartender had spat in, watching him drink it without complaint.

Before that: Roy Mercer, alive, standing in the doorway of the derelict basement telling Martin that Gil Marsh had been innocent, that Martin had already killed the real man responsible a year ago, that Martin himself was the memory-blind stranger in the file he'd been narrating down a payphone for weeks. Martin didn't believe him. He burned the photographs of Gil that night and wrote *he is lying to you* across Roy's face in black ink, then copied the plate number from Roy's car onto a scrap of paper.

Before that: Gil Marsh dying slow in that same basement, whispering a name—*Elias*—that meant nothing to the man strangling him, and Martin taking the dead man's suit, the dead man's keys, driving off in a car that wasn't his into a life that wasn't his either.

Before that: an anonymous voice on a motel phone giving him a name and a street. *Gil Marsh. That's your man.* Martin wrote it beside five other facts already inked on his skin.

Before that: the same call, earlier in it, Martin narrating a case file he barely remembered writing—Elias Prine, a man who denied giving his wife her insulin, who Martin himself had once ruled a liar.

Before that: Martin alone in a field at dusk, burning a hairbrush and a stack of paperback novels, grieving a wife he could no longer picture without a photograph, weeping for reasons that would be gone by morning.

Before that: Martin building his system—photographs pinned to motel walls, notes stapled to his own sleeves, tattoos climbing his arms and thighs—all in pursuit of a man known only by two initials, R.M., who had once split his skull open in his own bathroom.

Before that, further back than his system could reach: two intruders in that bathroom, his wife screaming, Martin's hands closing around one man's throat before something struck him and the world became a room he had to relearn every single day.

Before even that: Elias Prine sitting across a desk from an insurance investigator named Martin Kray, describing an amnesia Martin found convenient and false, a claim Martin denied with the clean certainty of a man who has never once forgotten anything—and, weeks later, Elias's wife testing her husband's broken memory with needle after needle, dying of the mercy he could not recall giving her.

And a year from now, in the basement again, blood cooling on concrete, Martin will photograph what he has done, write nothing new on his skin, and forget, within minutes, that he was ever right.

Danny Roarke was bleeding out on the concrete floor of the warehouse when he started thinking about the toilet.

Not this one—a different one, months back, small and fluorescent-lit, where Pruitt had made him say the story over and over until it stopped sounding like a lie. "You were in the men's room at the bus depot," Pruitt kept saying, pacing, sipping cold coffee. "You saw the deal go down. Tell it again. Tell it like you were there." And Danny had told it again and again, shaving off the hesitations, sanding the edges smooth, until the fabricated bust felt more real to him than his own childhood. That was the price of getting in.

It had worked. He remembered performing it for Bram in the back room of the social club, Bram's son Cal leaning against the wall with his arms crossed, and Mr. Ash watching him with the flat patience of a man deciding whether to trust a stranger. Danny had told the story like a memory, and at the end Bram had smiled and said, "Welcome aboard, Mr. Elm."

Trees. All of them trees. Bram's idea, some superstition about names carrying luck. Mr. Birch had complained about his—"Why do I gotta be the sissy one"—while they ate eggs and argued, of all things, about whether a certain pop song was about heartbreak or about God, and whether the waitress deserved twenty percent for bad coffee. Ren Vasco had walked in on that argument fresh out of prison, four years of silence bought and finally repaid, and Bram had clasped his hand like a brother.

None of that mattered now. What mattered was that the robbery had fallen apart in under a minute—alarms, a security guard who wasn't supposed to be armed, Mr. Ash putting three rounds through the windshield of a pursuing cruiser as they peeled away. Danny remembered running afterward, lungs burning, hijacking a car at a stoplight, the driver's face gone white with terror, the gun going off between them almost by accident. Danny had felt the punch of it in his own stomach a half-second before he pulled his own trigger.

Ash had gotten him to the warehouse, had held him and told him, voice cracking, that he wasn't going to die, not like this, not on some floor in the middle of nowhere. Birch had come stalking in soon after, ranting about an informer, insisting the whole job had been dirty from the start, and had gone out back to bury the diamonds in the weeds before anyone could search him.

Then Cedar arrived, grinning, popping the trunk of his car to reveal a kidnapped patrolman named Doyle, wrists zip-tied, eyes huge. Cedar had turned the radio on, some warped oldie crackling through static, and danced while he worked—the knife, the ear, the gasoline he poured over Doyle's shaking shoulders, laughing at his own joke the whole time.

That was when Danny, gut-shot and half-conscious, had raised his arm and shot Cedar dead where he stood.

He'd told Doyle then—no reason left to hide it—that he was a cop, that there were more coming, that Bram's whole crew was already surrounded. Doyle had wept with relief. Then Cal walked in, listened to Danny's account without expression, and put a bullet through Doyle's skull anyway, erasing the only witness.

Bram arrived last, surveying the carnage, and looked at Danny with something like grief. "Elm's the rat," he said quietly. Ash wouldn't have it—turned his gun on Bram instead, screaming denial—and in the three-way collision of bullets that followed, Bram fell, then Cal, then Ash took one through the shoulder.

Now, on the floor, with sirens rising outside, Danny finally said it plainly. "I'm a cop, Ash."

Ash's face didn't even change. He raised the gun and fired.

The warehouse doors burst open, light and noise flooding in, and the last thing Danny heard, sinking, was Ash going down under it, and somewhere far off, the ghost of that toilet-room story, still being told.

They found him alone at Silvermount, in the great unfinished hall, the snow globe shattered on the marble beside his hand. On his lips, the last word he ever spoke: "Bluebell." The newsreel men came within the week, cutting together footage of railcars and ribbon-cuttings, of the Clarion's masthead and a governor's race lost by a landslide, of a soprano's disastrous debut. The obituary ran eleven minutes and never once explained what he meant.

The paper sent a young reporter named Nash to find out. He went first to the seaside nightclub where Nora Kell was singing badly to a half-empty room, and when he asked her about the word she threw a glass at him and told him to get out, that she'd said everything she had to say about Emmett Rusk the day she left him.

So Nash went looking elsewhere, and the story came to him in pieces, out of order, the way old men and bitter women give up their memories.

He read Barrow's memoir first, a banker's dry account of a boarding-house deal struck when a defaulted lodger's mine deed made a miner's widow rich overnight, and she signed her son over to him like a note payable. Barrow wrote almost fondly of the sled that had driven into his stomach, of the small furious boy taken east anyway.

Marsh remembered the day, years later, when that boy turned twenty-five and inherited it all, and asked for nothing but a failing newspaper called the Clarion. Marsh had watched him move into the building, hire away a rival paper's entire staff, throw a party with a brass band and a chorus line, print a signed statement of principles on the front page like a boy nailing his name to a tree.

Devlin, sober now in another city, told Nash about the marriage—Emmett coming home engaged to Adele, the governor's niece, after a buying trip abroad, and then the long breakfasts afterward, husband and wife behind separate newspapers, not speaking. Devlin remembered the mud on Emmett's coat the day he mentioned a shopgirl named Nora Kell, and the rooms he began visiting in secret. He remembered Halloran bringing Adele to those rooms mid-campaign, the threats, Emmett's refusal to withdraw, the election lost, the marriage over, and his own request for a transfer that Emmett had granted without argument, as if relieved to lose one more thing.

Devlin's voice changed when he spoke of Nora's debut—the humiliation of it, her voice cracking under weight it was never built to carry, and how he, drunk, had started writing the review that damned her, and how Emmett had finished it himself, printed it, and fired him for the words they'd both put on the page.

Nora, when Nash caught her sober enough one evening, spoke of the poison she'd swallowed rather than sing again, and how Emmett had finally let her stop—too late, she said, far too late. She told him about Silvermount, the half-finished palace with its endless mirrors, where she'd sat working jigsaw puzzles in a hall built for parties that never came. She told him about the beach picnic that ended in a quarrel, about packing her bags.

The butler Colm filled in what came after: Emmett wrecking her bedroom in a fury, finding a glass snow globe among her things, murmuring that one word before he carried it past all those mirrors like a man carrying a relic.

Nash wrote it all down and could make no single shape of it. A boy, a fortune, a paper, a wife, a mistress, a ruin. He went back to Silvermount one last time, where workmen were clearing the grounds, and watched them shovel the wreckage of an old sled—paint chipped, the word BLUEBELL still legible on its side—into the furnace with the rest of the debris.

No one word explains a life, he wrote, and filed the story unfinished, the way it had come to him.

I hold hands with a woman I never dated, in a room lined with glass, on the top floor of a building about to become debris, and the pain in my cheek is a bright, structural fact, like the charges wired into the pillars below us. This is where it ends. But I should tell you how it starts, because the order doesn't matter anymore. Nothing here happens in order.

Before any of it, I was a man who investigated dangerous appliances by day and couldn't sleep by night. I found that the only cure was other people's grief, so I sat in circles for diseases I did not have and cried until I was empty enough to close my eyes. It worked until Ada Vey started showing up, faking her tears so badly that she made mine impossible.

On a flight not long after, I met a man selling soap out of a briefcase. Rex Marrow. I took his card and forgot him, the way you forget everyone on a plane, until my apartment turned to fire and particleboard dust and I had nowhere else to call.

He put me up in a gutted house at the edge of the district where nothing was zoned anymore. Outside a bar one night he asked me to hit him as hard as I could, and I did, and he hit me back, and something in that parking lot felt more honest than anything in my life since childhood. It became weekly. It became a basement. It became rules, and then it became more men than I could count, all wanting to feel their own faces stop being numb.

Ada came back into it sideways — she overdosed, and Rex carried her into the house and nursed her back, and then the two of them started an affair so loud I lay awake listening to the walls, which was funny, because I hadn't slept in years and now sleep was the one thing I couldn't get near their noise.

Rex had his soap operation too — fat skimmed from a surgery clinic's waste, boiled down and sold at eighty dollars a bar to the very stores that had thrown it out. He burned my hand with lye once, held my wrist there when I tried to float away into meditation, told me to stay in my body for once.

I blackmailed my employer with my own ruined face — paid to disappear, which suited me, since disappearing was becoming the only thing I was good at.

The club stopped being a club. Rex called it Havoc, filled the house with men who shaved their heads and did as they were told, breaking into offices, defacing what needed defacing. Then, one night, driving, he turned the wheel into oncoming traffic, let the car roll, and by the time I crawled out he was gone, as if the crash had taken only him.

Later — and here is where the story runs ahead of itself, the way it always does when I try to tell it straight — a man named Ogden is shot on an operation I didn't sanction, and I go city to city trying to shut down what I started, except every city already has a Havoc, and every man in every basement calls me Rex Marrow when I walk in.

I understood then. There was no Rex. There was only me, awake in the day, absent at night, doing with my sleep what I couldn't do with my waking hours. Ada told me the same thing, gently, the way you tell someone their house has already burned: she had been sleeping with him because he was me.

And Havoc had been busy while I dreamed — the debt towers, mined floor to floor, and I ran through them trying to cut wires with hands that didn't remember tying them. Rex met me on the stairs and beat me down them one flight at a time, and at the bottom I put the gun in my own mouth and pulled the trigger sideways through my cheek, because killing him meant wounding the only body we shared.

So we come back to the window, Ada's hand in mine, the shaven boys gone, the timers already run out beneath us, the glass about to become weather.

THE DOG

Tigre had killed before Ruben ever thought to profit from it. The rottweiler belonged to Nestor, but it was Ruben who noticed the animal's stillness before violence, the way it studied other dogs the way a man studies a debt he intends to collect. Ruben began entering him in the pit fights behind the tannery, and Tigre won, and won, until the promoter Chaco decided the dog's luck had gone on long enough and put a bullet in him in the ring. Ruben stabbed Chaco for it and ran with his friend Pipo into the night, and it was in that flight, blind with panic, that he ran the red light and drove into a stopped car at full speed.

The car belonged to Celine Vaz, a model whose face hung forty feet tall above the avenue where her lover Hector had installed her in a flat with a view of her own billboard. She woke in the hospital with pins holding her leg together and no memory of the crash, only of her lapdog Chispa left behind in the apartment. Chispa fell through a gap in the floorboards while she lay in traction, and Hector spent nights tearing up planks looking for the animal while Celine's leg blackened past saving. They took the leg. Later they took the billboard down too, rolled up like something embarrassing, and Hector's visits grew shorter until they stopped.

At the junction that night, before the ambulances came, a vagrant named Cardo had been sitting against a wall with nowhere else to be. He saw the wrecked rottweiler bleeding in the road and pulled it free of the metal simply because it was there and dying and he had nothing better to do with his hands. He fed it in the weeks after, nursed it among the other strays he kept, called it nothing because names were for things you meant to keep, though he kept it anyway.

Cardo had once fought in the hills with a rifle and a cause, and now fought for money instead, whatever the job required. Elian, a businessman with a brother he wanted gone, hired him to kill Sergio, the half-brother who co-owned everything Elian believed should be his alone. Cardo abducted Sergio easily enough but did not kill him — chained him instead in the ruined building where he lived among his dogs, fed him from the same pot he fed himself, and could not say why he waited. Eventually he brought the two brothers face to face, set a loaded pistol on the table between them, and walked out having taken payment from both men, leaving them to decide what blood was worth.

He had a wife once, and a daughter. He watched the wife's burial from across the cemetery, unwilling to be seen, and afterward followed his grown daughter Perla home at a distance, learning the shape of a life he had abandoned. He came back another night and broke into her flat while she was out, left a long confession on her answering machine — who he was, what he'd done, why he had never come before — and took a photograph of the room she lived in, as if it proved something.

The dog, meanwhile, had not stopped being what it was. While Cardo was away seeing to the brothers, the rottweiler killed every stray in the yard, methodical, unhurried, and Cardo came home to the bodies and put the gun to its skull and stood there a long time before lowering it. He could not do it. He told himself this was mercy and did not examine it further.

Back in the cramped house where it started, Nestor was shot dead robbing a bank, and at his funeral Alma, bruised in ways that no longer showed, refused Ruben's last offer to run. She had already run once, taking the baby and Ruben's savings with Nestor, and there was nothing left in Ruben's offer she wanted.

Cardo shaved, put on clean clothes, left money on Perla's table without waking her, and walked out into the wasteland at the edge of the city with the dog beside him, the two of them going nowhere in particular, which suited them both.

The helicopters came at night, low over the rooftops, trailing their mist of pesticide through every sleeping street, so that by morning a fine dust lay on windowsills across the whole city. Neil Hartigan stood at one such window knotting his tie while his wife Bess pinned her hair, both readying themselves for the dinner party they were hosting that evening, neither of them yet aware of the small disasters gathering elsewhere.

Across town Otto Kemp wiped flour from his hands and wrote down an order in his ledger: a birthday cake for a boy named Charlie Rill, seven candles, blue icing. He didn't know yet that he would never be paid, that the cake would sit in his window like an accusation.

That same morning Charlie was walking to school when a car driven by a tired waitress named Rhona clipped him at the crosswalk. He got up, brushed off his knees, told her he was fine, and walked the rest of the way home insisting nothing was wrong. By evening he had collapsed into a coma, and his parents Grant and Elaine began their vigil in a hospital corridor that smelled of antiseptic and vending-machine coffee. It was there that Grant's estranged father Duff appeared, unshaven, and confessed to an affair decades old, as if grief had loosened something in him that pride had kept locked for years.

Unpaid for his cake, ignored when he called to ask about it, Otto began making anonymous calls to the family's house at night, his voice thick with a menace he didn't fully understand himself.

Meanwhile Cheryl sat in her living room talking men through their fantasies over the phone while her husband Stu sat beside her, saying nothing, his jaw tight. Days later Stu and three friends drove out to fish and found a young woman floating face down in the river. They tied her to the bank with a rope and kept fishing for two more days before anyone was told. Vern's wife Iris, who worked children's parties as a clown, learned what they'd done and could not look at her husband the same way again.

In another part of the city the singer Vida performed nightly at a small club while her daughter Bee, a cellist, played alone in their house, practicing scales to an empty room. Officer Rowe, meanwhile, was lying to his wife Peg about a woman named Nan, and in the tangle of his lies he abandoned the family dog on a roadside to cover his tracks. Nan's ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot who flew the very crop-spraying routes over the city, learned she had a new man and took a saw to her furniture in a fury that left splinters across her floor.

House-sitting for the Hartigans, Ike and Dot amused themselves photographing Dot made up as a corpse, laughing at their own morbid joke in borrowed rooms.

At the dinner party Bess, flushed with wine, admitted to a nude modelling session years ago and an affair that followed it; Neil rose from the table and made a scene that emptied the room of guests.

Charlie died that night in the hospital. Grant and Elaine, hollowed out, went to the bakery to confront Otto for his calls, and instead found him crying over the counter, feeding them warm bread as though grief could be handed across like dough.

Bee found her mother asleep on the couch, closed the garage door quietly, and let the car run.

At a picnic in the hills, far from all of it, Stu raised a rock and brought it down on a young woman's skull.

That night a tremor moved through the whole city, rattling windows, spilling cups, and by the ten o'clock news every death and every wreck — Charlie, Bee, the girl by the river, the girl in the hills — had folded into one long, grey bulletin, read without pause, as if it had all happened at once.

The old man stood at the window with his hands folded behind his back, watching the flashing lights below paint the wet street red and blue.

"Nothing survives time," he said to the younger man beside him. "Not love, not anger, not the shape of a single night. It all gets worn down, eventually, like a coin in a pocket. You'll understand that better than most, given what you've just seen."

Below them, police were dragging two handcuffed men out of a club called the Pit, their shirts torn, one man's face slick with something dark that wasn't entirely his own blood.

They had been carried out that way—Cort first, then Jonah—shoved into the back of a van while a small crowd watched with the particular hunger of people who love watching other men fall.

An hour before, inside the Pit, Cort had torn through the crowd with a violence that didn't belong to him, grabbing a stranger by the collar, screaming a name that wasn't even the right one. The man's arm had snapped audibly, wet and simple, like a branch underfoot. Jonah had come up behind with a fire extinguisher already swinging, and it did not take long before the man's face stopped being a face. Somewhere in the back of the room, unnoticed, unbothered, a thin man with pale eyes—the one they called the Adder—watched it happen to someone else and smiled faintly, as if watching a play written just for him.

They had been sold his name for forty pounds by two men outside a bar who wore the casual boredom of people who trade in this sort of thing often. "The Adder," they'd said. "You want him, he'll be at the Pit." Cort had believed them.

Before that, there had been an ambulance, its doors thrown open, its lights sweeping the underpass walls, and Lise being lifted onto a stretcher with her head wrapped and her eyes closed, and Cort and Jonah stumbling out from the party into that scene without understanding it, without any way of understanding it.

Before that, in the underpass, the Adder had been beating a transsexual woman against the tiled wall, his knuckles catching the light strangely, and when Lise walked in on it he had simply turned, unbothered, and decided she would do just as well. He raped her there in the tunnel and slammed her skull against the concrete while a man walking his dog paused at the far end, looked, and turned quietly back the way he came.

Before that, Lise had left the party alone, disgusted, stepping past Cort as he pressed his mouth to some other woman's neck, high and drunk and laughing in that loose animal way he had. She'd taken the underground crossing instead of waiting for the light, because it was faster, because she didn't want to stand there a moment longer with the party's noise behind her.

Before that, the three of them—Lise, Cort, Jonah—had ridden the underground together, arguing about sex, about drinking, about nothing, laughing in that easy cruel way people laugh when they still believe they have time.

Before that, Lise had sat in a park in summer, sprinklers turning lazy arcs over the grass, children shrieking through the water, a book open on her knees and one hand resting, without her quite noticing, on the small curve of her stomach.

Before that, alone in the flat, she had watched a thin blue line resolve itself on a plastic stick and had sat down slowly on the edge of the bathtub, not crying, not yet.

And before all of it, in bed with Cort in the gray hour before morning, she had described a dream to him—a tunnel, red-walled, endless—while they teased each other lazily about Jonah, about old loves, about nothing that mattered yet.

"You see," the old man said, still watching the street empty of everyone now, the ambulance long gone, "she dreamed it before it happened. That's the strange thing about time. It doesn't warn you kindly. It just shows you the tunnel, and lets you walk into it anyway."

The gun dealer laughed at Nadir's accent while Sahar counted out the cash, and Nadir told himself he was only buying protection for the shop, nothing more.

Later—though Nadir did not yet know how much later—a detective named Isaiah Reece would kneel over a body dumped by a roadside ditch and pull back a tarp to find his own brother's face. That scene belonged to a night still weeks ahead, but it was already fixed, waiting, the way a photograph exists in the dark before it is printed.

Trey and Kwame took Halstead's car outside the restaurant with the practiced calm of men who had done it before. Halstead stood on the curb shaking, his wife's hand over her mouth.

Officer Boyle pulled over the Hobarts on a dark stretch of road and put his hands on Renee while her husband Clay watched, forced into stillness by the badge and the gun. Boyle's partner Voss sat frozen in the passenger seat, saying nothing, though soon enough—that same week—he would go to their commander and ask for a new car, because he could not stomach another shift beside the man.

Mateo came to change the Halsteads' locks, and Paula watched him from the top of the stairs like he might steal the silverware on his way out, muttering to her husband that she didn't trust him, not with that tattoo. Mateo said nothing. He drove across town and did the same work for Nadir, replacing the lock, warning him that the door itself was rotten at the frame, that a lock meant nothing on wood that soft. Nadir called him a thief trying to drum up more work and sent him off.

That same door gave way three nights later. Nadir's shop was stripped bare, glass on the floor, and when he called the insurance company they told him he'd been warned, that the claim was void, that this was his own failure.

Boyle, off duty, begged an insurance clerk named Delia Frank to authorize treatment for his dying father. She said there was nothing she could do. He left her office and did not go home for hours.

Then came the wreck—Renee's car flipped and burning, and Boyle, the same man who had put his hands on her weeks before, crawling in through broken glass to drag her out by the collar before the flames reached the seats.

Before that, though not before in the telling: Trey and Kwame ran down a shopkeeper named Pham with a stolen car and left him outside the hospital doors like a delivery. And before that too, in a scene that would only later make sense to anyone watching, Trey found Pham's van still packed with people locked in the dark behind the front seats, and instead of selling them on, he broke the locks himself and walked them down to the docks and told them to run.

Clay was caught trying to take back his own car, hands on the hood, officers circling with weapons drawn, and it was Voss—newly transferred, newly resolved—who talked the others down. Clay drove off with Trey in the passenger seat, outran the sirens, then stopped and threw him out onto the pavement like refuse.

Voss, driving alone at night, picked up a hitchhiker who turned out to be Kwame, and when the boy reached into his pocket for nothing more than a phone, Voss put him down and burned the car after, and told himself it had been necessary.

That was the body Reece would kneel over. That was the brother his mother would later say he never once went looking for, her voice flat with a grief that had turned to blame.

Nadir waited outside Mateo's house with the gun loaded with what he believed were real rounds, and fired as the man's daughter Rosie ran laughing into her father's arms — and the girl stood untouched, because Sahar had swapped the bullets for blanks without telling him, and Nadir wept and called her his angel.

Paula fell down her own stairs months later and told her housekeeper, gripping her hand, that Alba was the only friend she had.

The first snow came, and in the white hush two cars collided on the corner, and the drivers stood shouting in the cold exhaust, the whole old argument beginning again.

Solly Two Coats and his crew walked into the diamond house in the northern port dressed like men who'd never sinned in their lives, robes clean, eyes downcast, and walked out with a stone the size of a knuckle and twice as much trouble.

Overseas, his cousin Marv got word and told him plain: bring it straight to the city, no detours, no cleverness.

That same week, in the city itself, Grigor the Nail was busy in two directions at once—telling Solly, through a runner, about a bookmaker's shop worth robbing, and telling the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno the very same thing, so they'd walk into it themselves.

Around then Halloway and Digby, who promoted fights for men who didn't like losing money, sent their boxer Pretty Sam out to a traveller camp to buy a caravan.

Sam never got the caravan. A bare-knuckle man named Finn laid him out cold over the price, and Halloway was suddenly a fighter short for a bout that Coldstone had already fixed in his head.

So Halloway put Finn in instead, swore up and down to Coldstone that the man would go down in the fourth round, and hoped for the best.

Solly landed in the city not long after, handed the stone to the fence Hersch, and went straight to the bookmaker's to put money on the fight he'd heard so much about.

There, Ike, Benno and a third man called Tulley made a mess of the job—took Solly's arm along with his case, and got chased off by Grigor's own men before they'd gone two streets.

In the ring, Finn put his man down in the first round, not the fourth, and Coldstone lost a fortune and beat that loss into Halloway with his fists.

Marv flew in around the same days, found Solly's flat empty and cold, and hired a bounty hunter named Ledge to find his cousin.

Grigor got to Solly first. He cut the arm off to get the case open and found, to his fury, that the stone wasn't inside it at all.

Ledge, meanwhile, traced the pawnbrokers to a back road, shot their car to ribbons, and took Ike and Benno both, along with whatever they were carrying.

Coldstone fed what was left of Solly to his pigs and told Halloway and Digby exactly what would happen to them if the second fight went the same way as the first.

Halloway and Digby leaned on Finn to go down in the fourth this time, and that same night Coldstone's men burned Finn's mother alive in her caravan to make sure he understood the stakes.

Grigor, hunting the stone, ambushed Ledge's car with Ike and Benno still inside it, and in the shootout that followed Ledge, Grigor, and Benno all ended up dead in the road.

Tulley, who'd slipped off earlier with nobody watching, got clean away with a dog that had swallowed the diamond somewhere along the chaos.

In the ring the second time, Finn knocked his man out again in the fourth round exactly as promised, and the travellers, who had not forgotten the caravan or the woman burned in it, came through the crowd and slaughtered Coldstone's men where they sat.

Halloway and Digby found Coldstone himself cowering behind his own bookmakers and shot him where he stood, and by morning the travellers had packed up and gone, tents and wagons and all, as if they'd never been there.

Weeks later a dog was handed in at a pet shop, sick and shivering, and coughed up a diamond onto the counter in front of two men who recognized it at once. Halloway and Digby stood there holding the stone that had cost an arm, a mother, a bounty hunter, two pawnbrokers, a fixer, and a gang boss, and neither of them said a word about what they meant to do with it.

Emlyn said he had known for four years, that his wife had told him on the trip abroad, and that he had never thought much of his friend's letters either. Wilder sat with the drink going warm in his hand and did not know what to say to that, so he said nothing, and Emlyn let the silence do what he'd come to do.

He had come the same evening, as soon as Wilder rang him in a state, some confused apologetic call made after midnight that Emlyn had answered as if he had been waiting by the telephone for years. Now he sat in Wilder's own drawing room, in the house where the whole thing had started at a party neither of them any longer discussed, and told him calmly that his wife had let slip, only that afternoon, that Emlyn had been publishing a writer Wilder represented and privately despised — a small, unbearable coincidence that seemed to amuse Emlyn more than anything else in the story.

That had been in a bar, two years after the rooms were given up, when Odile told Wilder her marriage was over and that she had spent the whole of the previous night confessing everything to her husband, as if confession were a service she performed on a schedule. Wilder had listened and felt the old rooms rise up around him again, though they had been empty for a long time by then — the crockery split between them, the lease surrendered, the affair having become, in its last months, a chore neither wanted to keep paying for.

Before that there had been the dinner at the married couple's house, the two men talking for two hours about racquet games and school sport while Odile sat with no part in it at all, as though she were furniture bought to match the room. And before that the long lunch, Emlyn drinking through it steadily, baiting Wilder about contemporary fiction with a relish that seemed, at the time, only appetite, never once naming the thing he already knew.

Before that Emlyn had gone abroad, to some pale foreign hotel, and asked at the desk about a letter held for his wife, addressed in a hand he recognised at once. He had not needed to ask twice. Odile confessed, plainly, without much drama, and Emlyn had said only that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife — a remark she carried home with her like a coin in her pocket, turning it over. She went back to the rented rooms and said nothing whatever about the trip, and the afternoon passed exactly as the others had, tea and the low light and Wilder's hand at her waist, as though nothing in the world had shifted.

Before that there had been months of ordinary contentment — the rooms furnished with linen and plates, a small domestic economy built out of an affair, so that it began to resemble a marriage more than the marriage itself did. Odile had told him she was carrying her husband's child, and they had decided, without much discussion, that the rooms would go on exactly as before, as if a pregnancy elsewhere were no more consequential than weather.

And before all of it, first in the telling but last in the living memory that mattered, there had been the party at Wilder's own house, the noise of other people's voices coming up through the floor, and Wilder leading her up the stairs to say that she was lovely, while below them glasses were filled and refilled and nobody thought to wonder where their host had gone.

Billy Pilgrim has come unstuck in time, and it is no use asking him what happened first, because he will only tell you what happened next.

He is standing at the podium in Chicago, an old man with a face like a wet paper bag, telling the crowd about the aliens and the fourth dimension, and the crowd is not listening, and then he is a boy in the small industrial town where he was born, weak and peculiar, and his father is throwing him into the deep end of a pool to teach him to swim, and he sinks to the bottom and sees, quite calmly, that this is not the worst thing that will happen to him, or the first.

He is on the zoo planet with the film actress, and the aliens are explaining, in their kind flat way, that every moment exists at once, that free will is a joke his species tells itself, and this does not surprise him, because he already knows he will be shot dead by a beam weapon after a speech, has always known it, the way you know the shape of a room you have lived in your whole life.

He is a chaplain's assistant shipped overseas with no training worth the name, and then he is lost behind enemy lines with a scout who beats him for wanting to be left to die, and then, without any of the connecting tissue that other men's lives seem to have, he is being held in a camp beside enemy officers who have drawn double rations for years through a clerical error, fat and pink among the starving, and it does not strike him as strange, because nothing does anymore.

He marries the daughter of the man who owns the optometry school and becomes rich, and this happens sometime, though he could not tell you when, before or after the city burns in one night and he comes up from the meat locker with the other prisoners to find it gone, a moonscape, and they are made to dig bodies from the cellars until one of the diggers dies of the dry heaves, retching up nothing, days on end, and Billy watches this the way he watches all of it, unstuck, un-anchored, a tourist in his own life.

The scout dies of gangrene on the prison train and blames him with his last stinking breath, and a fellow prisoner promises, almost gently, to have him killed one day on the dead scout's account, and Billy nods, because he already knows how he will die and it will not be that way, though he cannot say if this promise comes before the beam weapon or after, or whether "before" and "after" mean anything at all where he is standing now, which might be the zoo, might be Dresden, might be Ilium.

He comes home and collapses and is hospitalised, and another patient introduces him to a hack science fiction writer who will later put words in his mouth that are almost, but not quite, his own. He survives a plane crash in the mountains, the only one who does, and his wife dies of carbon monoxide driving too fast to the hospital, and he cannot say which grief came first, the loss of her or the loss of altitude, because in his head they arrive together, always together, a single bright collapsing moment.

His daughter decides he is senile and takes his affairs out of his hands, and this feels to him like something that happened long ago and also something that has not happened yet. He goes on the radio and tries again to tell them: everyone is always alive, no one is ever dead, the dead are only in a bad condition at a particular time. The audience laughs, or does not laugh; he cannot be sure of the order of things, even his own sentences.

And then he is at the podium in Chicago again, or for the first time, finishing his speech, and the beam comes, and he goes, and it happens exactly as he has always known it would, which is to say: not first, not last, but simply, everywhere, always.

He marries the daughter of the man who owns the optometry school and becomes rich, and this happens sometime, though he could not tell you when, before or after the city burns in one night and he comes up from the meat locker with the other prisoners to find it gone, a moonscape, and they are made to dig bodies from the cellars until one of the diggers dies of the dry heaves, retching up nothing, days on end, and Billy watches this the way he watches all of it, unstuck, un-anchored, a tourist in his own life.

The scout dies of gangrene on the prison train and blames him with his last stinking breath, and a fellow prisoner promises, almost gently, to have him killed one day on the dead scout's account, and Billy nods, because he already knows how he will die and it will not be that way, though he cannot say if this promise comes before the beam weapon or after, or whether "before" and "after" mean anything at all where he is standing now, which might be the zoo, might be Dresden, might be Ilium.

He comes home and collapses and is hospitalised, and another patient introduces him to a hack science fiction writer who will later put words in his mouth that are almost, but not quite, his own. He survives a plane crash in the mountains, the only one who does, and his wife dies of carbon monoxide driving too fast to the hospital, and he cannot say which grief came first, the loss of her or the loss of altitude, because in his head they arrive together, always together, a single bright collapsing moment.

His daughter decides he is senile and takes his affairs out of his hands, and this feels to him like something that happened long ago and also something that has not happened yet. He goes on the radio and tries again to tell them: everyone is always alive, no one is ever dead, the dead are only in a bad condition at a particular time. The audience laughs, or does not laugh; he cannot be sure of the order of things, even his own sentences.

And then he is at the podium in Chicago again, or for the first time, finishing his speech, and the beam comes, and he goes, and it happens exactly as he has always known it would, which is to say: not first, not last, but simply, everywhere, always.
